### Problem: Keys and Rooms {#sec-gr-p2-keys}

There are `n` rooms numbered $0..n-1$. `rooms[i]` is the list of keys found in room $i$. Start in room $0$. Each key opens the room of that number. Return whether every room can be visited.

**Graph model.** Directed. The list `rooms[i]` is already the adjacency list of arcs $i \to k$ for each key $k$ in the room. The edge points from the room to the key, in that direction.

**Invariants.** A room is counted when it is opened, which is when it is first discovered. The answer is whether the discovery count equals $n$. Keys are not vertices.

**Approaches.**

1. **Stack** — mark room $0$, then push each unseen key. $O(n + m)$ where $m$ is the total number of keys.
2. **Recursion** — the same mark-first walk. Safe at the constraint $n \le 1000$.

#### Stack

::: {.form-next}
`rooms` is the adjacency list. Count a room when its mark flips from unseen to seen.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("keys", "stack")
    assert str(final) == "True"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def can_visit(rooms):
    n = len(rooms)
    seen = [False] * n
    seen[0] = True
    st = [0]
    opened = 1
    while st:
        u = st.pop()
        for v in rooms[u]:
            if not seen[v]:
                seen[v] = True
                opened += 1
                st.append(v)
    return opened == n


assert can_visit([[1], [2], [3], []]) is True
assert can_visit([[1, 3], [3, 0, 1], [2], [0]]) is False
assert can_visit([[]]) is True
```

##### C++

```cpp
bool canVisitAllRooms(vector<vector<int>>& rooms) {
    int n = rooms.size(), opened = 1;
    vector<char> seen(n);
    seen[0] = 1;
    vector<int> st = {0};
    while (!st.empty()) {
        int u = st.back();
        st.pop_back();
        for (int v : rooms[u]) if (!seen[v]) {
            seen[v] = 1;
            opened++;
            st.push_back(v);
        }
    }
    return opened == n;
}
```

:::

#### Recursion

::: {.form-next}
The same discovery rule, written as a function of the room.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("keys", "rec")
    assert str(final) == "True"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def can_visit_rec(rooms):
    n = len(rooms)
    seen = [False] * n

    def go(u):
        seen[u] = True
        total = 1
        for v in rooms[u]:
            if not seen[v]:
                total += go(v)
        return total

    return go(0) == n


assert can_visit_rec([[1], [2], [3], []]) is True
assert can_visit_rec([[1, 3], [3, 0, 1], [2], [0]]) is False
for n in range(1, 8):
    for _ in range(20):
        rooms = [[j for j in range(n) if j != i and random.random() < 0.4] for i in range(n)]
        assert can_visit(rooms) is can_visit_rec(rooms)
```

##### C++

```cpp
int visitRoom(int u, vector<vector<int>>& rooms, vector<char>& seen) {
    seen[u] = 1;
    int total = 1;
    for (int v : rooms[u])
        if (!seen[v]) total += visitRoom(v, rooms, seen);
    return total;
}

bool canVisitRec(vector<vector<int>>& rooms) {
    vector<char> seen(rooms.size());
    return visitRoom(0, rooms, seen) == (int)rooms.size();
}
```

:::

:::

**Worked trace.** Second sample: room $0$ offers keys $1$ and $3$. Room $1$ offers $3, 0, 1$, all already open or the same. Room $3$ offers $0$. Room $2$ still holds the only key to itself, and nobody visited it. Three rooms open, four exist.

**Edge cases.** One room and an empty key list: already inside, true. A room whose only key is itself, and that room is not $0$: it stays shut. A key that points back at $0$ adds no new room.

**Pitfalls.** Reversing the arc, from the key back to the room that contained it, walks the second sample into room $2$ and returns true. Counting keys instead of rooms returns a number that can exceed $n$ when one room holds several keys, and can be smaller than $n$ when the last room holds an empty list even though it was opened.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **The arc points backwards.** An edge from the key to the room that held it answers "what reaches room $0$?". The second sample then walks into room $2$ and returns true.
- **Counting keys.** On $[[1], [0]]$ every key is counted, including ones already used, and the total is $3$ against two rooms. Only a room whose mark flips is a new room.
- **Room $0$ starts shut.** A counter that begins at $0$ waits for some room to contain the key $0$. Room $0$ is open before the loop.
- **Every room appears in some list.** That is an in-degree test. The second sample passes it and is still false: the key to room $2$ sits in room $2$.
:::

**Variants.** The smallest set of starts that reaches every room, when the graph is a DAG, is [LC 1557 · Minimum Number of Vertices to Reach All Nodes](https://leetcode.com/problems/minimum-number-of-vertices-to-reach-all-nodes/){difficulty="Medium"}. Summing the size of the reach set of every start is [AC abc204_c · Tour](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc204/tasks/abc204_c). Several rooms open at the beginning is the same search with those rooms pushed first. A key that breaks after one use is no longer a room graph: the state has to remember which keys are in hand (@sec-gr-p4).

Source: [LC 841 · Keys and Rooms](https://leetcode.com/problems/keys-and-rooms/){.solved difficulty="Medium"}
